steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a short paper on estimating position bias from click data when the (item, position) data is sparse, using item embeddings. Motivate the problem from learning to rank and click models, explain the sparsity issue we hit in production carousel ads, and list our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Learning to rank, click data, and position bias
- Click models and the PBM
- Why PBM rather than the cascade model (carousel ads)
- Our experience with regression EM in production
- The sparsity problem
- Proposed approach and contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- L2R improves ranking in search, recommender systems, targeted ads (refs)
  - click data = implicit feedback, unlike explicit ratings; contains biases incl. position bias
  - position bias: location influences chance of selection; prior work: debias / denoise clicks
- Click-Modeling
  - PBM: P(click) = P(examine position) [position bias] x P(click | examined) [item-user relevance]
- Focus: position bias under PBM
  - cascade model well studied but assumes linear examination order
  - carousel ads w/ navigation buttons: left arrow -> right-to-left; right arrow -> left-to-right
- Production experience
  - accurate position bias critical, else biased relevance estimates
  - regression EM in production carousel ads, logged click data, no effect on real traffic
  - didn't work well: training data sparsity
- Sparsity
  - REM input: (item, position) tuples; ideally items spread over all positions
  - marketers use fixed order -> items in few positions; often one item always in one position
  - 15 ads -> only 6.7% of (ad, position) combinations observed
- Approach
  - item similarities fill missing (item, position) entries; similar item X' for (item X, position 1)
  - embeddings preserving similarity; LSI and VAE not tested much for this -> use them as initial proposal
- Contributions
  - new problem: sparsity in (item, position) pairs
  - method w/ LSI and VAE
  - experiments on public + internal data: REM w/ item embedding more accurate, better L2R
  - LSI > VAE

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Learning to Rank (L2R) is a useful approach for improving ranking performance in search engines, recommender systems, and targeted advertisement. Click data from ranking applications is a promising source for improving personalized rankings. Click data is different from explicit feedback like user ratings, because it reflects how users interact with applications, and this makes it a valuable kind of implicit feedback. But because it is implicit, click data has various biases, and one of them is position bias. Position bias means that where content is located influences how likely users are to select it. To get reliable signals out of users' implicit feedback, previous research has focused on removing the bias, or in other words denoising the click data.

One approach to these issues is Click-Modeling. For example, the position-based click model (PBM) represents the probability that a user clicks on an item as the product of two probabilities: the probability that the user examines a specific position (position bias), and the probability that the user clicks on the item after examining it (item-user relevance).

In this study we focus on estimating position bias with the PBM approach. The cascade model has been studied a lot, but it assumes that items are examined in a linear order, and this may not apply in all industrial scenarios where the examination order is not linear or follows a specific pattern, for example carousel ads with navigation buttons. With carousel ads with navigation buttons, when users click the left arrow button, the ads shown shift to the left, and users examine the ads from right to left. If they click the right arrow button instead, the order is reversed and users examine the ads from left to right.

How accurate the position bias estimation is matters a lot for the performance of recommender systems, because a wrong estimation leads directly to a biased evaluation of item-user relevance. We implemented the regression EM algorithm in the production carousel advertisement to estimate position bias from logged click data, without affecting real user traffic. Unfortunately, we found that this model did not work well for this application, because the training data for the position bias estimation was sparse.

Sparsity problem:
- REM input = (item, position) tuples; ideally items evenly over all positions, enough samples
- real world: marketers use fixed pre-determined order -> most items in only a few positions; often one item always in one position
- 15 ads on our e-commerce platform -> only 6.7% of (ad, position) combinations observed; estimation suffers

Proposed approach:
- item similarities to estimate missing values in (item, position) matrix; (item X, position 1) missing -> use similar item X'
- embeddings that preserve item similarity
- LSI and VAE not tested much for this -> initial proposal

Contributions:
- new problem: data sparsity in (item, position) pairs
- method using LSI and VAE
- experiments on public and internal datasets: REM with item embedding more accurate, better L2R
- LSI outperforms VAE

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Learning to Rank (L2R) is a useful approach for improving ranking performance in search engines, recommender systems, and targeted advertisement. Click data from ranking applications is a promising source for improving personalized rankings. Click data is different from explicit feedback like user ratings, because it reflects how users interact with applications, and this makes it a valuable kind of implicit feedback. But because it is implicit, click data has various biases, and one of them is position bias. Position bias means that where content is located influences how likely users are to select it. To get reliable signals out of users' implicit feedback, previous research has focused on removing the bias, or in other words denoising the click data.

One approach to these issues is Click-Modeling. For example, the position-based click model (PBM) represents the probability that a user clicks on an item as the product of two probabilities: the probability that the user examines a specific position (position bias), and the probability that the user clicks on the item after examining it (item-user relevance).

In this study we focus on estimating position bias with the PBM approach. The cascade model has been studied a lot, but it assumes that items are examined in a linear order, and this may not apply in all industrial scenarios where the examination order is not linear or follows a specific pattern, for example carousel ads with navigation buttons. With carousel ads with navigation buttons, when users click the left arrow button, the ads shown shift to the left, and users examine the ads from right to left. If they click the right arrow button instead, the order is reversed and users examine the ads from left to right.

How accurate the position bias estimation is matters a lot for the performance of recommender systems, because a wrong estimation leads directly to a biased evaluation of item-user relevance. We implemented the regression EM algorithm in the production carousel advertisement to estimate position bias from logged click data, without affecting real user traffic. Unfortunately, we found that this model did not work well for this application, because the training data for the position bias estimation was sparse.

The input data of the regression EM algorithm is the tuple (item, position). Ideally, items should be spread evenly over all positions with enough samples. But in real-world scenarios marketers often show advertisements in a fixed order decided in advance, so most items are only placed in a few positions. Also, in many cases we see that one item is always placed in a single position. When we have 15 ads in our e-commerce platform, it means we observe only 6.7\%(=15/15^{2}) of all combinations of (ad, position) tuples. The position bias estimation suffers from this.

In this study we propose a method to deal with this sparsity issue. Our approach uses item similarities to estimate the missing values in the (item, position) matrix. For example, when the (item X, position 1) entry is missing, we estimate its position using a similar item X^{\prime}. For this, we use embedding techniques to make a representation that preserves the similarity between items. We found that item embeddings for estimating position bias have not been tested much with well-known tabular embedding baseline models like Latent Semantic Indexing (LSI) and Variational Autoencoder (VAE). So we use these two models as an initial proposal in this study.

In summary, the key contributions of our study are:

- • We introduce the new problem of data sparsity in (item, position) pairs for position bias estimation in a real-world scenario.

- • We propose a new method for estimating position bias using Latent Semantic Indexing and Variational auto-encoder.

- • We run extensive experiments on public and internal datasets, which show that our method, REM with item embedding, estimates position biases more accurately and improves learning-to-rank performance.

- • We find that LSI is better than VAE for the accuracy of position bias estimation and for personalized ranking.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Learning to Rank (L2R) [1] is a valuable approach to improving ranking performance in search engines, recommender systems [2] [3], and targeted advertisement [4]. Click data from ranking applications is a promising source for enhancing personalized rankings. Unlike explicit feedback such as user ratings, click data reflects users' interaction with applications, which makes it a valuable form of implicit feedback. However, because of its implicit nature, click data contains various biases, including position bias [5]. Position bias means that the location of content influences its likelihood of being selected by users. To extract reliable signals from users' implicit feedback, previous research has focused on removing this bias, in other words, on denoising click data.

Click-Modeling is one approach to addressing these issues. For instance, the position-based click model (PBM) [6] represents the probability of a user clicking on an item as the product of two probabilities: the probability that the user examines a specific position (position bias), and the probability that the user clicks on the item after examining it (item-user relevance).

In this study, we focus on estimating position bias under the PBM approach. While the cascade model [7] has been extensively studied, it assumes a linear order of examining items and may not apply to all industrial scenarios, where the order of item examination may not be linear or may follow a specific pattern, such as in carousel ads with navigation buttons. In that case, when users click the left arrow button, the displayed ads shift to the left, so users examine the ads in right-to-left order. Conversely, if they click the right arrow button, the order of examination is reversed and users examine the ads from left to right.

Accurate position bias estimation is critical for the performance of recommender systems, because an inaccurate estimation directly leads to a biased evaluation of item-user relevance. We implemented the regression EM algorithm [8] in the production carousel advertisement to estimate position bias from logged click data, without affecting real user traffic. Unfortunately, we found that this model did not work well for this application due to training data sparsity in the position bias estimation.

The regression EM algorithm takes the tuple (item, position) as input. Ideally, items should be evenly distributed across all positions with a sufficient number of samples. In real-world scenarios, however, marketers often display advertisements in a fixed pre-determined order, so most items are placed in only a few positions. Moreover, in many cases one item is consistently placed in a single position. With 15 ads in our e-commerce platform, this means that we observe only 6.7\%(=15/15^{2}) of all combinations of (ad, position) tuples, and the position bias estimation suffers from it.

In this study, we propose a method to address this sparsity issue. Our approach uses item similarities to estimate missing values in the (item, position) matrix. Specifically, when the (item X, position 1) entry is missing, we estimate its position using a similar item X^{\prime}. To do so, we employ embedding techniques to create a representation that preserves the similarity between items. We found that item embeddings for estimating position bias have not been tested extensively with well-known tabular embedding baseline models such as Latent Semantic Indexing (LSI) [9] and Variational Autoencoder (VAE) [10]. We therefore leverage these two models as an initial proposal in this study.

In summary, our study makes the following key contributions:

- • We introduce the novel problem of data sparsity in (item, position) pairs for position bias estimation in a real-world scenario.

- • We propose a novel method for estimating position bias using Latent Semantic Indexing and Variational auto-encoder.

- • We conduct extensive experiments on public and internal datasets, which demonstrate that our method, REM with item embedding, estimates position biases more accurately and improves learning-to-rank performance.

- • We find that LSI outperforms VAE in the accuracy of position bias estimation and in personalized ranking.

References:
